analysis.one_liner: Opens cargo shipping between Hawaii and the mainland to lower-cost foreign-flag vessels.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in July 2003, never got a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: A federal law called the Merchant Marine Act requires all cargo shipped between U.S. ports to travel on ships built in the United States, registered in the United States, and staffed largely by American crews. That makes shipping goods to and from Hawaii far more expensive. This bill would carve out an exception for Hawaii's trade, letting foreign-built, foreign-registered ships carry that cargo as long as they meet U.S. labor, environmental, and safety standards and employ U.S. crews where required. It also gives seamen injured on the job clearer access to U.S. courts and lets their employers opt into a workers' compensation system.
analysis.who_benefits: Hawaii consumers and businesses, who pay some of the highest shipping costs in the country because so few U.S.-flagged, U.S.-built ships serve the islands. The bill also benefits foreign shipping companies that could enter the Hawaii trade, and it strengthens legal remedies for injured seafarers.

how_it_helps.text: Exempts Hawaiian noncontiguous trade from the requirement that cargo between U.S. ports move only on U.S.-flagged vessels, allowing foreign qualified freight vessels to carry that cargo [S2][S3].
Lets the Secretary of Transportation document foreign-built, foreign-registered vessels for Hawaiian trade if they employ U.S. citizens as required [S3].
Subjects all vessels in the coastwise trade, foreign or domestic, to minimum international labor standards for seafarers and to U.S. and international environmental standards [S2][S3].

Gives seamen injured by employers with no U.S. office the right to sue in the U.S. district court nearest where the injury happened, and lets employers elect coverage under the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: U.S. shipbuilders and U.S.-flag shipping companies serving Hawaii, notably Matson, would face new lower-cost competition. American merchant mariners in the Hawaii trades could see wages and job security squeezed as foreign operators pay international-standard wages. Seamen could also see their Jones Act remedy for employer negligence replaced by a fixed workers' compensation schedule if their employer elects it.

drawbacks.text: Opening Hawaii's trade to foreign vessels could reduce demand for U.S.-built ships and U.S.-flag crews, weakening the domestic maritime industrial base that the Merchant Marine Act was designed to protect [S2][S3].

The bill lets an employer elect Longshore Act coverage, making that remedy exclusive and replacing the seaman's right to sue the employer for negligence, which could reduce compensation in some injury cases even as it adds jurisdictional protections [S3].

Allowing documented foreign qualified vessels to shift to foreign registry without the Secretary's approval, with only a $10,000 civil penalty in place of forfeiture, loosens controls on vessels entering and leaving the U.S. registry [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Lower shipping costs would directly help Hawaii households and businesses, and the bill pairs the opening with labor, environmental, and legal protections for seafarers. The real tradeoff is strategic: a domestic fleet and shipyard base, kept alive partly by Hawaii's protected trade, would shrink, and U.S.-flag crews could lose premium jobs. Whether the savings reach consumers depends on competition actually materializing among foreign carriers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and a subcommittee, never got a hearing or a floor vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ed Case introduced the bill on July 24, 2003, and it was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure and Armed Services Committees [S1][S5].
The next day it was referred to the Transportation subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, where no further action was taken [S5].
The bill had no cosponsors and never advanced beyond committee referral before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S.-flag shipping lines and shipbuilders kept their protected Hawaii trade. Hawaii consumers kept paying the higher shipping rates the bill aimed to reduce.

for.name: Rep. Ed Case
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the House floor the day after introduction.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support or opposition cannot be determined from the record.

industries.industry: U.S.-flag ocean shipping carriers serving Hawaii
industries.note: Carriers holding the protected Hawaii trade would face foreign-flag competition able to operate with cheaper ships and crews, cutting their freight premiums. Their gain has come at the cost of high shipping prices for Hawaii consumers.
The Jones Act's build requirement keeps orders flowing to U.S. shipyards; letting foreign-built ships serve Hawaii would erode part of that protected demand.
Foreign operators could enter the Hawaii trade with lower-cost vessels, subject to U.S. labor, environmental, and crewing standards in the bill.

industries.industry: American merchant mariners in the Hawaii trades
industries.note: U.S. crews could face wage and job pressure from foreign competition, but the bill extends minimum international labor standards and preserves crew-employment requirements for documented foreign vessels.
